title: How CRISPR Could Rewrite Human DNA
description: A bacterial immune system became a word processor for genes. How CRISPR works, how it cured sickle cell disease, and the hard questions it raises, told in 3D animation.

shots.line: Inside almost every cell of your body is a set of instructions, three billion letters long. Your DNA.
A single wrong letter in that code can cause a devastating disease.
For most of history, there was nothing we could do about it. Then, scientists found a tool that can find any spot in the genome, and cut it, with incredible precision.
It's called CRISPR. And it was borrowed from bacteria.

texts.text: HOW IT COULD REWRITE HUMAN DNA

shots.line: DNA is a long, twisted ladder. Each rung is a pair of chemical letters: A, T, G and C. Their order spells out genes, the recipes for making proteins.
If you printed out the DNA in one human cell, it would fill around two hundred thick phone books. And if you stretched it out, it would be about two metres long.
Just reading it was a colossal task. The Human Genome Project took thirteen years and about three billion dollars, finishing in two thousand and three.
Some diseases, like sickle cell disease, come from a single misspelled letter in a single gene.
In sickle cell disease, red blood cells bend into stiff crescent shapes. They get stuck in blood vessels, causing terrible pain and organ damage.

It affects millions of people around the world, many with African, Middle Eastern or South Asian ancestry. Strangely, carrying one copy of the gene helps protect against malaria, which is why it became so common.
For decades, scientists dreamed of fixing faulty genes directly. But the early tools for editing DNA were slow, expensive, and hard to aim.
Tools called zinc fingers and TALENs could be built to cut chosen spots, but designing each one could take months of specialist work.
The answer came from somewhere unexpected. In the nineteen nineties, a Spanish microbiologist named Francisco Mojica was studying microbes from salt marshes.
In their DNA, he noticed strange repeated sequences, separated by unique spacers. A Japanese team led by Yoshizumi Ishino had first spotted similar repeats in nineteen eighty seven.
He and colleagues named them CRISPR: clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats.

texts.text: C  R  I  S  P  R

shots.line: Around two thousand and five, Mojica worked out what the spacers were: snippets of DNA from viruses that had attacked the bacteria before.
Bacteria are in a never-ending war with viruses called phages. Phages are thought to be the most numerous biological entities on Earth, outnumbering bacteria by around ten to one.
CRISPR was an immune system. The bacteria kept a library of mugshots of their enemies.
If the same virus attacked again, the bacteria copied the matching mugshot into a short strand of RNA. That strand guided a cutting protein to the virus's DNA, and chopped it up.

In two thousand and seven, Rodolphe Barrangou, Philippe Horvath and colleagues at the yoghurt company Danisco confirmed it, while trying to protect the bacteria they used to make yoghurt and cheese from viruses.
The most important cutting protein is called Cas nine.
It comes from Streptococcus pyogenes, the bacterium that causes strep throat.
In two thousand and eleven, the French microbiologist Emmanuelle Charpentier met the American biochemist Jennifer Doudna at a conference in Puerto Rico. They decided to work together.
Charpentier was working in Sweden, Doudna in California. They collaborated across nine time zones, by email and video calls.
In June twenty twelve, they published a landmark paper. They showed that Cas nine could be reprogrammed with a guide RNA to cut any DNA sequence they chose.
Here's how it works. Scientists write a short guide sequence, about twenty letters long, that matches the target.
Cas nine slides along the DNA. When the guide finds its perfect match, Cas nine cuts both strands of the double helix.
The cell then rushes to repair the break. Scientists can use that moment to switch a gene off, or to slip in a new, corrected piece of DNA.
It's like a word processor for genes: find, cut, and replace.
Within months, teams led by Feng Zhang and George Church showed that it worked in human cells too.
CRISPR was cheap, fast and easy. Labs all over the world began using it almost overnight.
The discovery also sparked a long legal battle, between the University of California, where Doudna works, and the Broad Institute in Massachusetts, over who owns the patents.
In twenty twenty, Charpentier and Doudna won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. It was the first time a science Nobel had been shared only by women.
The first big medical success came for sickle cell disease.
Doctors take a patient's own blood stem cells, and use CRISPR to switch on a gene for a type of haemoglobin we all make before we're born.
Those edited cells are put back, and begin making healthy red blood cells.
Victoria Gray, from Mississippi, was the first American with sickle cell disease to be treated this way, in twenty nineteen. Her pain crises stopped.
In late twenty twenty three, regulators in Britain and the United States approved the treatment, called Casgevy. It was the world's first approved CRISPR medicine.
Scientists are now testing CRISPR against inherited blindness, high cholesterol, some cancers, and other genetic diseases.

Newer versions are even more precise. Base editing, invented in David Liu's lab in twenty sixteen, can change a single letter without cutting both strands. Prime editing can search and replace short passages.
CRISPR has even been turned into fast diagnostic tests, which can detect the genetic material of viruses, like the one that causes COVID nineteen.
In twenty twenty five, doctors in Philadelphia treated a baby boy named KJ, born with a rare and deadly liver disorder, with a gene-editing therapy designed just for him.
CRISPR is also changing farming. Researchers are using it to make crops that resist disease, survive drought, or simply keep fresh for longer.
Some scientists want to use it to spread genes through wild mosquitoes that stop them carrying malaria, a disease that kills hundreds of thousands of people every year.
In twenty twenty four, surgeons in Boston transplanted a kidney from a gene-edited pig into a living patient, part of a push to solve the shortage of organs for transplant.
But CRISPR also raises hard questions.
Editing a patient's blood cells affects only that person. But editing an embryo would change every cell, including eggs and sperm, so the changes would pass to future generations.
In twenty eighteen, a Chinese scientist, He Jiankui, announced that he had secretly edited the DNA of human embryos, and that twin girls had been born.
Scientists around the world condemned it as reckless and unethical. He was sentenced to three years in prison.
The twins were known by the names Lulu and Nana. He was released in twenty twenty two, and the long-term effects of his edits on the girls are still unknown.
Most countries now ban or tightly restrict editing embryos for pregnancy. Deciding where the limits should be is a question for all of us, not just scientists.
There are other worries, too. CRISPR can sometimes cut the wrong place. And the first approved treatment costs over two million dollars per patient in the United States, so who can afford it?
A defence system that bacteria evolved to fight viruses has become one of the most powerful tools in the history of medicine.
We can now rewrite the code of life. The question is no longer whether we can. It's how wisely we choose to.
